title: Suspensions & Colloids
subtitle: You already know one settles and one does not. This is why.
objectives: Use particle size to place a mixture as a solution, a colloid or a suspension
Explain why a suspension settles and a colloid does not
Name the five kinds of colloid and give an example of each
Explain why the Tyndall effect happens, not only that it happens

cards.title: Last term you learned the test. Now the reason
cards.text: A suspension settles. A colloid does not. True. But it is a symptom, not the cause. The cause is size.

cards.title: Three bands, measured in nanometres
cards.text: A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Everything here is decided by how big the scattered bits are.
points: **Solution:** under 1 nm. Single molecules or ions.
**Colloid:** 1 nm to 1000 nm. Too big to dissolve, too small to fall.
**Suspension:** over 1000 nm. Big enough for gravity to win.
**Same substance** can be any of the three. It is the size, not the stuff.

cards.title: Sand, salt, milk
cards.alt: Three glasses side by side: sandy water with visible grains, clear salt water, and opaque white milk
cards.text: One settles, one is invisible, one is opaque and never settles. Three different things.

cards.title: Gravity pulls on everything. It only wins sometimes
cards.text: Water molecules are moving and they bombard anything floating in them, millions of times a second.
points: **A suspension particle** is heavy enough that gravity beats the bombardment.
**A colloid particle** is light enough that the knocking keeps it up.
**That random knocking** has a name: Brownian motion.
**Nothing is holding it up.** It is being hit from every side at once.

question.text: Why does a colloid not settle?
options: Its particles are light enough that molecular bombardment keeps them up
Gravity does not act on particles that small
The liquid is too thick for anything to sink
Its particles dissolve into the liquid
question.explain: Gravity still pulls on them. The constant knocking from moving liquid molecules just wins.

cards.title: Your blood does both, depending on what you do to it
cards.text: Blood is red cells carried in plasma. Leave it alone in a tube and the cells sink.
points: **Standing still**, red cells settle out and leave straw-coloured plasma above.
**Doctors measure that**, and how fast it happens says something about inflammation.
**In your veins** it never settles, because it never stops moving.
**Plasma itself** is a colloid. Proteins too small to fall out.

cards.title: Floodwater is brown because it is a suspension
cards.text: Fast water carries soil and sand. The water is not dyed. It is holding solid pieces.
points: **Moving water** keeps heavy particles up by sheer force.
**When it slows**, gravity wins and the silt drops out.
**That is how** river deltas and flood plains get built.
**Volcanic ash** is the same idea in air: solid specks held up in a gas.

question.text: Floodwater is brown because the soil has dissolved in it.
question.explain: Not dissolved. Suspended. The pieces are still whole, and they drop out when the water slows.

cards.title: Size decides everything
points: Under 1 nm dissolves. Over 1000 nm falls. Between the two, it floats.
Settling is the symptom. Particle size is the cause.

cards.title: A colloid is a size, not a substance
cards.text: Anything can be a colloid if its pieces land in that band. Solid, liquid or gas, in solid, liquid or gas.

cards.title: Five colloids, named by what is spread in what
cards.text: Named by what is spread through what. Two quiz questions come from this.

cards.title: Oil and water, made to stay mixed
cards.text: Shake oil and water and it separates in seconds. An emulsifier is what stops that.
points: **An emulsifier molecule** has a water-loving end and an oil-loving end.
**It sits on the boundary** of every droplet, holding the two apart.
**Egg yolk does this** in mayonnaise. That is the whole trick.
**Without one**, the droplets find each other and merge back.

cards.title: Why you shake a paint can and not a fuel can
cards.text: Car paint is pigment held in liquid. Petrol is a solution. One separates on the shelf, one never does.
points: **Pigment** is solid and big enough to settle. Shake it or you spray clear liquid.
**Metallic paint** carries aluminium flakes. The sparkle is suspended metal.
**Petrol** is dissolved, under a nanometre. Shaking it changes nothing.
**Medicine bottles** say shake well for exactly the paint reason.

question.text: What does an emulsifier actually do?
options: It makes the droplets heavier so they sink
It reacts with the oil to make a new substance
It sits on the droplet boundary so the droplets cannot merge
It dissolves the oil into the water
question.explain: One end likes water, the other likes oil. It parks on the edge and keeps the droplets apart.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Two parts done. The light part is next, and it is the best one.

cards.title: The Tyndall effect, and the reason behind it
cards.text: Shine a torch through a solution and you see nothing. Through a colloid and the beam appears.

cards.title: Particles the size of the light itself
cards.text: Visible light has a wavelength around 400 to 700 nanometres. Look at that number again.
points: **Colloid particles are 1 to 1000 nm**: the same ballpark as the light.
**Something that size** scatters light sideways, so you see the beam.
**Solution particles** are far too small to interfere with it.
**That is the test:** a visible beam means colloid or bigger.

cards.title: Same beam, two tanks
cards.alt: A light beam invisible in a tank of plain water and clearly visible as a shaft in a tank of milky water
cards.text: Plain water on the left: nothing to see. Add a little milk and the beam appears.

cards.title: God rays are this effect, drawn on purpose
cards.text: Those shafts of light through a window or a forest canopy are a rendering of real scattering.
points: **In the real world** the beam shows because dust or mist is scattering it.
**Clean air shows nothing.** No particles, no visible shaft.
**Engines call it** volumetric lighting, and it is expensive to draw.
**Switch fog off** in the settings and the shafts go with it.

question.text: Why does a colloid never settle out?
options: The particles are small enough to stay suspended
question.explain: Too small for gravity to win against the jostling of the liquid around them.

cards.title: Fog lights point down for a reason
cards.text: Fog is a colloid. Water droplets in air. Your headlights light up the fog instead of the road.
points: **Main beams scatter** off the droplets and glare straight back at you.
**Fog lights sit low** and aim down, under most of the scattering.
**Full beam in fog** makes it worse, not better.
**Same physics** as the torch in the colloid. Just inconvenient.

question.text: Why can you see a torch beam in fog but not in clear air?
options: Clear air absorbs the light completely
Fog droplets are about the size of light's wavelength and scatter it sideways
Water glows faintly when light hits it
Fog is denser, so light travels slower
question.explain: Scattering, not glowing. The droplets throw light sideways into your eye, so the beam shows.

terms.def: Particles 1-1000 nm spread through another substance. They do not settle.
Particles over 1000 nm. Left alone, they settle out.
Random knocking by moving molecules that keeps colloid particles up.
A colloid of one liquid inside another, like milk.
A molecule that sits on a droplet's edge and stops an emulsion separating.
Light scattering off colloid particles, which makes the beam visible.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Size sets the class: under 1 nm, 1-1000 nm, over 1000 nm.
Suspensions settle because gravity beats the bombardment.
Colloids come in five kinds, named by what is in what.
A visible beam means the particles are colloid-sized or bigger.

quiz.text: Which size range makes a mixture a colloid?
quiz.explain: Below 1 nm it dissolves. Above 1000 nm it settles. In between, it stays spread out.
quiz.objective: Use particle size to place a mixture as a solution, a colloid or a suspension

options: its particles dissolve and then fall
its particles are heavy enough for gravity to beat molecular bombardment
quiz.explain: Gravity acts on every particle. In a suspension it wins; in a colloid the knocking wins.
quiz.objective: Explain why a suspension settles and a colloid does not

quiz.text: Milk is which kind of colloid?
quiz.explain: Fat droplets spread through water. Liquid in liquid, which is an emulsion.
quiz.objective: Name the five kinds of colloid and give an example of each

quiz.text: Whipped cream is mostly air held in liquid. That makes it a…
quiz.explain: Gas in a liquid is a foam. Most of its volume is air.
quiz.objective: Name the five kinds of colloid and give an example of each

quiz.text: Fog is water droplets floating in air. Which kind of colloid is that?
quiz.explain: Anything dispersed in a gas is an aerosol. Fog is liquid in air, smoke is solid in air.
quiz.objective: Name the five kinds of colloid and give an example of each

quiz.text: Brownian motion means the particles are swimming under their own power.
quiz.explain: They are being knocked about by moving liquid molecules. Nothing is powering them.
quiz.objective: Explain why a suspension settles and a colloid does not

quiz.text: What does an emulsifier do to two liquids that normally separate?
options: Coats each droplet so the droplets cannot join back up
Thickens them both until nothing can move
quiz.explain: A water-loving end and an oil-loving end let it sit on every boundary and hold them apart.

quiz.text: Why does a torch beam show up in a colloid but not in a solution?
options: Colloid particles are close to the wavelength of light and scatter it sideways
Colloid particles give off their own light
quiz.explain: Scattering, not absorbing or glowing. Visible light is 400-700 nm, right in the colloid band.
quiz.objective: Explain why the Tyndall effect happens, not only that it happens

quiz.text: Why do car fog lights sit low and point down?
options: Because fog scatters a high beam straight back at the driver
quiz.explain: Fog is a colloid. Aim a main beam into it and the glare comes back at you.
quiz.objective: Explain why the Tyndall effect happens, not only that it happens

quiz.text: Why does a paint tin need shaking but a tank of petrol does not?
options: Paint pigment is a suspension that settles; petrol is a solution
quiz.explain: Pigment particles are big enough to sink. Dissolved petrol is under a nanometre and cannot.
quiz.objective: Use particle size to place a mixture as a solution, a colloid or a suspension

quiz.text: Left standing in a tube, blood separates into red cells and plasma.
quiz.explain: Red cells are big enough to settle. How fast they do is a real medical measurement.
quiz.objective: Explain why a suspension settles and a colloid does not

quiz.text: Which of these would NOT show the Tyndall effect?
quiz.explain: Dissolved salt is under a nanometre. Far too small to scatter light. The other three are colloids.
quiz.objective: Explain why the Tyndall effect happens, not only that it happens

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 1 Science. The scope says Suspensions & Colloids, which Term 1 Week 8 already introduced. He can already apply the settling test and name the Tyndall effect. So this week supplies the mechanism underneath both rather than repeating the definitions: the nanometre bands that decide the class, Brownian motion as the reason a colloid stays up, the five colloid types as a size band that any two states of matter can occupy, and scattering as the reason the beam shows. The fog-light and paint-tin cards exist because they are the two places he will meet this outside a test.
discussion: Why can the same substance be a solution, a colloid or a suspension?
Blood never settles inside you. Why does it settle in a tube?
Fog lights point down. What would happen if they pointed up?
extension: Shine a phone torch through milk, then through salt water, in a dark room. Only one shows the beam.
Leave muddy water in a glass overnight and mark where the line forms.
misconceptions: That suspended means dissolved. Suspended particles are whole and can be filtered out.
That Brownian motion is the particles moving themselves. They are being knocked.
That the Tyndall effect is the liquid glowing. It is light being thrown sideways.
